procedural_history.originating_court: Magistrate Court (implied, based on the complaint under the Insecticides Act and reference to Section 482 Cr.P.C.)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 08.08.2016 of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM-M 4458/2016.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed a petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. in the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh (CRM-M 4458/2016) seeking to quash a complaint filed under the Insecticides Act. The High Court dismissed the petition on 08.08.2016.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed the High Court's judgment to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 653 of 2017) and vacated the interim relief.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the petition to quash the criminal proceedings pending against the appellants in respect of misbranded insecticide under the Insecticides Act, 1968.

facts: The appellants were facing criminal prosecution under the Insecticides Act, 1968, for an alleged 'misbranded' insecticide.
They petitioned the High Court to quash these proceedings, arguing that mandatory provisions of the Act were violated, causing them prejudice.

Their main arguments were that a spare sample was sent for analysis to the Central Insecticides Laboratory (CIL) before the formal complaint was filed, and they were not given a separate opportunity to exercise their right to have the sample analyzed.
The High Court dismissed their petition, and the appellants appealed to the Supreme Court.
law: Under the Insecticides Act, 1968, particularly Section 24(4), an accused person has the right to adduce evidence to controvert the report of a State Insecticide Analyst.
This right is typically exercised by requesting that a third sample of the insecticide be sent to the Central Insecticides Laboratory (CIL) for testing.
The report from the CIL is considered conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the options available to an Insecticide Inspector after a state-level analysis finds an insecticide to be misbranded.

The Court determined that the Inspector has two valid courses of action: 1) Launch a criminal prosecution and submit the third sample to the court, allowing the accused to then request CIL testing, or 2) Send the third sample to the CIL for analysis upon a request from the person from whom it was collected, even before filing a formal complaint.

The Court found that there is no prohibition in the Act against sending the sample to the CIL before filing a complaint. In fact, doing so can be beneficial to the accused, as a favorable CIL report might prevent prosecution altogether.

In this specific case, the CIL analysis had already been performed. The Court reasoned that since the CIL report is conclusive and was already available, the right under Section 24(4) had been addressed.

The purpose of producing the sample in court is to enable the accused to ask for a CIL test. Since that test had already been done, the failure to produce the sample in court did not prejudice the appellants or vitiate the proceedings.
The Court concluded that the criminal prosecution must proceed on the basis of the existing, conclusive CIL report.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal, holding that the High Court was correct in dismissing the petition to quash the criminal proceedings. The Court found no procedural error, as the appellants' right to have the sample tested by the CIL had been effectuated, and the prosecution could validly proceed based on the conclusive CIL report.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the petition to quash the criminal proceedings pending against the appellants in respect of misbranded insecticide under the Insecticides Act, 1968.
appellant_arguments: The spare sample was sent for analysis to the Central Insecticides Laboratory (CIL) before a formal complaint was filed in court.

Under Sections 22(6)(ii) and 24(4) of the Act, the spare sample should have been submitted with the complaint, and only the court where the complaint is lodged can direct its analysis at the request of the accused.
By sending the sample for analysis pre-complaint, the appellants were deprived of their statutory right to request the analysis themselves.
This denial of a valuable right to adduce evidence to controvert the initial insecticide analyst's report vitiates the entire prosecution.

The appellants cited the cases of Mis B.R. Agrotech and another vs. State of Haryana and State of Punjab vs. National Organic Chemical Industries Ltd. to support their claim of being denied their right to reanalysis.
respondent_arguments: The non-production of the third sample along with the complaint does not invalidate the prosecution launched against the appellants.
The purpose of producing the third sample in court is to enable the accused to apply for analysis from the CIL, but only if this has not already been done.
By operation of law (Section 24(4)), the report from the CIL is conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein.
Therefore, the High Court's conclusion to dismiss the petition for quashing the prosecution is unassailable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The report of an Insecticide Analyst is conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein, unless the person from whom the sample was taken exercises their right to challenge it by notifying their intent to adduce evidence in controversion, as per the statutory procedure.
obiter: The respondent, without availing of the remedy of a report by the Director of the Central Insecticides Laboratory (CIL), may not be entitled to plead deprivation of the statutory defence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The right of an accused under Section 24(4) of the Insecticides Act, 1968, to request the court to send a sample for analysis to the Central Insecticides Laboratory (CIL) is not absolute. This right is extinguished if the sample has already been tested by the CIL, regardless of whether this was done before or after the formal complaint was filed. The resulting CIL report is conclusive evidence, and the prosecution can proceed on that basis without the accused having a further right to seek re-analysis.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory interpretation of Section 24(3) and Section 24(4) of the Insecticides Act, 1968, based on the plain and unambiguous meaning of the text.
why_appellant_lost: The right of an accused to request the Magistrate to send the third sample to the CIL for testing can be exercised only if the complaint is founded on the report of the State Insecticide Analyst and a CIL report is not already available.
The opening words of Section 24(4), 'Unless the sample has already been tested or analysed in the CIL', explicitly preclude the accused's right to request analysis if a CIL report already exists.

The appellant's argument that they were deprived of a statutory right is incorrect because the right they claim to exercise (requesting analysis from the court) does not endure once a CIL report has been obtained.
Accepting the appellant's view would entail rewriting the provisions of the Act, which are plain and unambiguous.
why_respondent_won: If the complaint is filed on the basis of a report from the CIL, the question of the accused exercising the right under Section 24(4) to request another analysis does not arise.
The purport of Section 24(4) is that the report of the CIL shall be conclusive evidence of the facts stated therein.
In cases where a CIL report is already obtained or available, the criminal prosecution must proceed on that basis.

The non-production of the third sample along with the complaint does not vitiate the prosecution, as its purpose is to enable the accused to apply for analysis from the CIL only if this has not already been done.
policy_considerations: Continuing the criminal complaint against the appellants would not be an exercise in futility or an abuse of the process of the Court, as the prosecution is based on a conclusive CIL report.
